text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- A working group of the Centre Party is looking at strategies which, for the first time since 1951, could permit the party to cooperate with a majority Social Democratic government, rather than campaigning for the formation of a non-socialist governing coalition.

- Swedish industry investment this year has broken all reacords, reaching 66 billion crowns which is the highest figure since Statistics Sweden started measuring the data in the 1930s. Transport and the chemical industries lead the investment by branch, with 60 percent and 40 percent increases respectively.

- Norway has recruited 450 health care workers from Sweden in a campaign aimed at filling up to 3,000 vacancies in its health care system. About 600 doctors are also needed but so far only four Swedes have decided to work there.

- Swedes' propensity for saving continues apace, with three out of four households intending to set aside at least as much now as during the last two years, according to a survey by the TCO civil servants' union edited by market research organisation Sifo. One interesting and possibly worrying phenomenon is that the 15-29 age group, traditionally big spending, seems to have changed attitude and begun saving more, TCO economist Anders Hahnel commented.

- Industries which depend heavily on electricity, together with the confederation of Swedish industries, are campaigning in favour of the country's 12 nuclear reactors with the message they are safe and should be allowed to continue operations. In contrast, certain reactors in the former Soviet Union are dangerous and should be shut down, according to the Swedish industries.

- Stockholm's hotel sector is about to overheat, with the first shortages appearing since the late 1980s but there are no plans for major investment. The centralised hotel telephone booking service, which was once used only by tourists, is now helping many Swedish businessmen to find hotel rooms in the capital.

- Finance Minister Erik Asbrink wants to allow the state pension funds numbers one to three to buy securities listed on the bourse. These funds at present deploy 550 billion crowns which are mostly invested in government bonds. A proposed new regulation on the funds can be ready by next summer.

- Norway has never imported so much energy from Sweden and Denmark as this year. So far Norway has imported six terawatts from abroad compared with the same time last year when it had exported roughly the same quantity. Soon the Norwegian transmission system will have reached full capacity and be unable to carry more imported power.

- Women are more adept at playing the stock market than men, according to the conclusions of Stockholm's Matteus brokerage. The best three stocks on a recent course were chosen by women, and a further three women figured in the top 10 performers, who were each given a theoretical 100,000 crowns to invest.
